Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. \section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Web-crawled corpora are the dominant source of pretraining data for large language models (LLMs), yet an increasing fraction of this data is itself LLM-generated.
Estimates suggest that 7--17\% of recent scientific papers and peer reviews contain substantial LLM-modified content \cite{mapping_llm_science,monitoring_ai_review}, and this proportion continues to grow as generated text enters the web and becomes seed material for subsequent generation.
The result is recursive generation chains whose outputs progressively diverge from human-written text---a problem that current detection methods are ill-equipped to address.

Existing detectors \cite{fast_detectgpt,binoculars,ld_score,detectgpt} provide binary real-vs-synthetic classification, forcing an all-or-nothing filtering decision: discard everything flagged as synthetic, losing potentially useful first-generation content, or retain everything, admitting text with compounding distributional drift.
This conflates qualitatively different material.
A first-generation continuation---an LLM expanding a human-written passage---retains much of the source distribution's lexical and structural properties.
A third- or fourth-generation text, conditioned recursively on prior LLM outputs, exhibits measurably reduced vocabulary diversity, compressed perplexity, and narrower token probability distributions.
Treating these as a single ``synthetic'' category discards provenance information that could inform risk-stratified curation decisions.

We argue that a finer-grained characterization is needed: \emph{ordinal depth estimation}, the task of classifying text into generation depth classes (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+) rather than producing a binary label.
No existing method addresses this task directly.
When repurposed as ordinal depth predictors, individual detection scores exhibit high cross-generator variance---confidence intervals spanning 0.59--0.82 in macro-F1 (\S\ref{sec:results-baselines})---making any single detector unreliable across unknown generators.
Concurrent work on iterative paraphrasing chains \cite{broken_telephone,markovian_chains} analyzes convergence behavior under semantic-preservation constraints, which bound distinguishable depth classes to approximately three.
These results do not extend to \emph{non-paraphrastic} generation chains (e.g., continuation), where the absence of semantic anchoring permits richer depth signal.

We study distributional drift in non-paraphrastic LLM generation chains across six generators from three model families (Pythia, OLMo, Qwen; 0.6B--8B parameters).
Our central empirical finding is \emph{differential depth response}: central-tendency and diversity features---including reference-model mean entropy (functionally an NLL-based out-of-distribution score \cite{ood_baseline}), type-token ratio, and hapax ratio---drift monotonically with generation depth, while distributional shape features (entropy standard deviation, tail decay) remain near-stationary.
This pattern is consistent with recursive generation inducing a location shift in the NLL distribution: text becomes progressively more predictable on average while the functional form of the distribution is preserved.
The combination of drifting and stationary features yields a 7-feature ensemble that achieves leave-one-generator-out (LOGO) macro-F1 of 0.79 (95\% CI [0.786, 0.799]; \textit{plan-014}), with per-generator held-out F1 ranging from 0.69 to 0.85.
This ensemble maintains tight cross-generator consistency (CI width 1.3\,pp), whereas the best single detector spans over 20\,pp (\textit{plan-015}).
The practical advantage is reliability across unknown generators, not just average performance.

We also report a negative finding.
Depth-aware data curation---selecting training data based on estimated generation depth---does not improve downstream language model quality compared to random subsampling at equal sample count (perplexity: 2.367 random vs.\ 2.387 depth-stratified; \textit{plan-004-v2}).
Depth fingerprinting is an effective \emph{diagnostic} tool for characterizing text provenance, not a \emph{curative} tool for data selection.

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
    \item \textbf{Task formulation.} We define ordinal generation depth estimation as a task beyond binary detection, providing a framework for finer-grained provenance characterization of web-crawled text.
    \item \textbf{Empirical characterization.} We document differential depth response across six generators spanning three model families (0.6B--8B): a 7-feature ensemble combining drifting and stationary features achieves LOGO F1\,=\,0.79 [0.786, 0.799], significantly outperforming all single-detector baselines ($p < 0.001$) with tight cross-generator consistency (\textit{plan-014, plan-015}).
    \item \textbf{Negative finding.} Depth-aware data curation does not outperform random subsampling for downstream CLM quality (size-matched 2.367 vs.\ depth-stratified 2.387; \textit{plan-004-v2}), establishing depth fingerprinting as diagnostic rather than curative.
\end{enumerate}

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows.
\S\ref{sec:related} surveys related work on text detection, model collapse, and data quality.
\S\ref{sec:method} describes generation chain construction, feature extraction, and evaluation protocol.
\S\ref{sec:results} presents classification results, differential depth response analysis, baseline comparisons, and the downstream utility experiment.
\S\ref{sec:discussion} discusses limitations and future directions.

Notably, adding Qwen3-8B data \emph{improves} classification on the original five generators (+0.9\,pp to 0.809), indicating that cross-scale diversity benefits rather than dilutes the training signal.

\paragraph{Cross-family generalization.}
Family-level leave-out (all Pythia generators held out, trained on OLMo + Qwen only) yields $\Delta$\,=\,+0.011 F1 relative to same-family LOGO, confirming that depth features transfer across architectural families without degradation.

Text length correlates weakly with depth (Spearman $|\rho| < 0.14$).
Length-normalized feature trends are preserved, and length-matched subsampling yields comparable or higher F1 ($\Delta$\,=\,+0.041), ruling out length as a confound (Appendix~\ref{app:length}).

\subsection{Differential Depth Response}
\label{sec:results-differential}

Features exhibit \emph{differential depth response}: central-tendency and diversity measures drift monotonically with depth, while distributional shape measures remain near-stationary.
This pattern is consistent with recursive generation inducing a location shift in the token-level NLL distribution---the text becomes progressively more predictable (mean shifts), while the functional form of the distribution is preserved (shape is invariant).

Individual-level Spearman correlations with depth confirm the split (Figure~\ref{fig:feature-drift}):
drifting features show strong monotonic trends (hapax ratio $\rho = -0.558$, TTR $\rho = -0.543$, entropy mean $\rho = -0.476$),
while shape features show weak or negligible correlations (entropy std $|\rho| = 0.076$, tail decay $|\rho| = 0.087$).

\paragraph{Feature complementarity.}
Table~\ref{tab:ablation} reports ablation results.
The full 7-feature set (F1\,=\,0.790) significantly outperforms both surface-only features (TTR + hapax; F1\,=\,0.729) and reference-only features (entropy statistics + tail decay; F1\,=\,0.745; McNemar $p \approx 0$).
Permutation importance ranks hapax ratio highest (0.271), followed by TTR (0.165) and entropy mean (0.156).
Surface features capture vocabulary impoverishment; reference features capture distributional shift---neither subsumes the other.

\paragraph{Cross-family reference models.}
To confirm that differential depth response is not an artifact of the Pythia-410M reference model, we compute features using three cross-family references: Pythia-410M, OLMo-2-1B, and Qwen3-0.6B.
All three achieve LOGO F1 between 0.80 and 0.82, with consistent drift directions across features.
The pattern generalizes across reference model architectures.

\subsection{Comparison with Detection Baselines}
\label{sec:results-baselines}

\label{tab:baselines}
\end{table}

The ensemble outperforms all baselines in mean F1: +3.9\,pp over Avg-LogProb ($p < 0.001$, $\Delta$ CI [3.4, 4.4]), +7.7\,pp over LD-Score, +17.1\,pp over FastDetectGPT, and +21.9\,pp over Binoculars (Table~\ref{tab:baselines}).

The critical distinction is \emph{reliability}.
The ensemble CI spans just 1.3\,pp [0.786, 0.799], while single-detector CIs span 18--26\,pp (e.g., Avg-LogProb [0.616, 0.820]).
A single detector's CI is wider than \emph{all pairwise detector differences}, meaning no single detector is reliably best across generators.
Each detector captures partial depth signal---Avg-LogProb tracks mean perplexity shift, LD-Score captures character-level distributional change---but each fails on specific generator families.
The 7-feature ensemble aggregates complementary signals, producing stable performance regardless of the held-out generator.


\subsection{Downstream Utility: A Negative Finding}
\label{sec:results-downstream}

Can depth-aware data curation improve downstream language model quality?
We fine-tune OLMo-2-0425-1B on five data variants (3 seeds each) and evaluate perplexity on a held-out test set (Table~\ref{tab:downstream}).

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{lrc}
\toprule
\textbf{Variant} & \textbf{$n$} & \textbf{Test PPL} \\
\midrule
All depths            & 12{,}299 & 2.335 $\pm$ 0.000 \\
Size-matched (random) & 3{,}951  & 2.367 $\pm$ 0.000 \\
Depth 0--1 only       & 3{,}951  & 2.387 $\pm$ 0.001 \\
Binary-filtered       & 3{,}951  & 2.389 $\pm$ 0.000 \\
Depth 0 only          & 797      & 2.681 $\pm$ 0.001 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Downstream fine-tuning perplexity (OLMo-2-0425-1B, mean $\pm$ std across 3 seeds). At equal sample count, random subsampling (2.367) outperforms depth-aware curation (depth 0--1: 2.387, binary-filtered: 2.389).}
\label{tab:downstream}
\end{table}

The results are unambiguous: data quantity dominates depth composition.
Training on all 12{,}299 samples yields the lowest perplexity (2.335).
At equal sample count ($n$\,=\,3{,}951), random subsampling (2.367) \emph{outperforms} both depth-stratified selection (depth 0--1: 2.387) and binary detection filtering (2.389).
Cross-seed variance is below 0.002 across all variants, confirming the robustness of this null result.

Restricting training to human-only text (depth 0, $n$\,=\,797) produces a sharp perplexity increase to 2.681, driven primarily by the 5$\times$ reduction in data volume rather than depth composition per se.

We report this negative finding transparently: depth fingerprinting is an effective \emph{diagnostic} tool for characterizing text provenance, not a \emph{curative} tool for data curation.
Knowing the generation depth of a document does not, by itself, make it more or less useful for training.

\begin{abstract}
As large language model (LLM) outputs accumulate on the web, training corpora increasingly contain recursively generated text of unknown provenance depth.
We formulate \emph{ordinal depth estimation}---classifying whether text is human-written (gen-0), first-generation synthetic (gen-1), or deeper (gen-2+)---a task that moves beyond binary real-versus-synthetic detection.
Existing detectors provide only binary scores and, when repurposed for ordinal prediction, exhibit high cross-generator variance (confidence intervals spanning 0.41--0.82), making them unreliable depth estimators.
We characterize a \emph{differential depth response} in distributional features computed under a held-out reference model: central-tendency and diversity features (entropy mean, type-token ratio, hapax ratio) drift monotonically with generation depth, while distributional shape features (entropy standard deviation, tail decay rate) remain near-stationary.
Combining both feature types into a 7-feature ensemble exploits this complementarity: the full set (macro-F1\,=\,0.80) outperforms surface-only (0.75) and reference-only (0.75) subsets.
In leave-one-generator-out evaluation across 6 generators from 3 model families (0.6B--8B parameters), the ensemble achieves macro-F1 of 0.79 (95\% CI: [0.786, 0.799]; $p < 0.001$ vs.\ all single-detector baselines), with per-generator held-out F1 ranging from 0.68 to 0.86.
However, depth-aware data curation does not improve downstream language modeling quality compared to random subsampling---data quantity, not depth composition, is the primary determinant---positioning depth fingerprinting as a diagnostic tool for provenance characterization, not a curative tool for data selection.

2	\label{sec:discussion}
3	
4	\paragraph{Why are shape features stationary?}
5	We observe that distributional shape features (entropy standard deviation, tail decay) remain near-stationary across generation depths, while central-tendency features drift monotonically (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}).
6	One \emph{speculative} explanation is that shape is primarily determined by the sampling mechanism (temperature, top-$p$ truncation) and the model's architecture-level output distribution, both of which are fixed across generation steps.
7	Recursive generation shifts \emph{what} the model talks about---steering toward higher-probability regions of the vocabulary---but does not alter \emph{how} the model distributes probability mass around its predictions.
8	If this account is correct, shape features should remain stationary even at much greater depths, while level features should continue to drift until reaching a fixed point.
9	We flag this as a hypothesis for future investigation, not a conclusion supported by our current experiments.
10	
11	\paragraph{Practical implications.}
12	The differential depth response enables risk-stratified data curation.
13	Rather than the binary keep-or-discard decision imposed by existing detectors, practitioners can flag gen-2+ text for manual review while retaining gen-1 content that preserves much of the source distribution's properties.
14	The tight cross-generator consistency of the 7-feature ensemble (CI width 1.3\,pp; \textit{plan-015}) makes this feasible even when the generating model is unknown---the typical scenario for web-crawled data.
15	
16	\paragraph{Information value of the negative finding.}
17	The downstream experiment (\S\ref{sec:results-downstream}) demonstrates that depth-aware curation does not improve language model quality over random subsampling at equal sample count (\textit{plan-004-v2}).
18	This negative result carries positive information value: it rules out depth-based filtering as a data selection strategy, sparing practitioners from investing in depth-conditional pipelines that would not yield quality gains.
19	The dominant factor is data quantity, not depth composition---a result consistent with scaling-law findings that emphasize the primacy of data volume \cite{self_consuming_mad}.
20	
21	\paragraph{Connection to model collapse.}
22	Our results relate to, but are distinct from, model collapse \cite{curse_of_recursion,strong_model_collapse,self_consuming_mad}.
23	Model collapse describes distributional degradation when models are \emph{retrained} on their own outputs across generations.
24	We observe analogous distributional drift---monotonic decrease in vocabulary diversity, compression of perplexity---in \emph{inference chains} without any parameter updates.
25	This suggests that the drift mechanisms documented in model collapse theory (regression toward high-probability modes, loss of distributional tails) operate at inference time as well, driven by the sampling process rather than gradient updates.
26	The shared phenomenology motivates using depth fingerprinting features as early indicators of data that, if used for retraining, may accelerate model collapse.

1	\section{Related Work}
2	
3	\subsection{AI-Generated Text Detection}
4	
5	A large body of work addresses binary classification of machine-generated text.
6	Statistical approaches exploit token-level probability signals:
7	\cite{gltr} use token rank histograms under a reference model,
8	\cite{detectgpt} identify machine text through negative log-probability curvature,
9	and \cite{fast_detectgpt} accelerate this via conditional probability curvature.
10	\cite{binoculars} contrast perplexity ratios between two similar models,
11	while \cite{dna_gpt} measure n-gram divergence after re-generation.
12	More recent work extends these ideas:
13	\cite{ld_score} introduce character-distribution signatures orthogonal to perplexity,
14	\cite{intrinsic_dimension} leverage embedding-space intrinsic dimensionality,
15	and \cite{diveye} capture token surprisal diversity patterns.
16	Learned approaches include generator-specific discriminators \cite{grover},
17	feature-augmented transformers for cross-domain transfer \cite{feat_aug_transformer},
18	and disentangled representations for cross-generator generalization \cite{generator_barrier}.
19	Robustness analyses show that paraphrase attacks severely degrade detectors \cite{reliable_detection,paraphrase_evades},
20	though detection remains information-theoretically feasible whenever human and machine distributions are distinguishable \cite{detection_possibilities}.
21	\cite{jawahar_survey} and \cite{release_strategies} provide broader surveys.
22	
23	These methods share a fundamental limitation: they produce a single binary score with no capacity for depth estimation.
24	When repurposed as ordinal depth predictors, individual detector scores exhibit high cross-generator variance (confidence intervals spanning 0.59--0.82 in our experiments), making them unreliable as standalone depth estimators.
25	Our reference-model entropy features are functionally NLL-based out-of-distribution scores \cite{ood_baseline}, drawing on the same signal backbone as DetectGPT and Binoculars.
26	The contribution is not the features themselves but rather the ordinal depth formulation, the empirical finding of differential depth response under recursive generation, and multi-feature complementarity that yields tight cross-generator consistency.
27	
28	\subsection{Model Collapse and Iterative Generation}
29	
30	Model collapse theory establishes that recursive training on synthetic data degrades generative quality.
31	\cite{curse_of_recursion} prove that iterative retraining causes irreversible distribution tail loss across VAEs, GMMs, and LLMs.
32	\cite{strong_model_collapse} show that even minimal synthetic data fractions suffice to trigger collapse,
33	\cite{self_consuming_mad} characterize precision--diversity trade-offs in autophagous loops,
34	and \cite{model_collapse_avoidable} demonstrate that data accumulation (rather than replacement) mitigates the effect.
35	These results concern \emph{training-loop} dynamics where model parameters change across iterations.
36	We study \emph{inference chains}: the same frozen model generates text recursively without retraining, yet distributional drift still accumulates.
37	
38	Two concurrent works study iterative generation directly.
39	\cite{broken_telephone} analyze LLM paraphrasing and translation chains, showing that information distortion accumulates with depth and outputs converge toward attractor states---critically, the semantic-preservation constraint of paraphrasing bounds depth-distinguishable classes to approximately three.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Web-crawled corpora are the dominant source of pretraining data for large language models (LLMs), yet an increasing fraction of this data is itself LLM-generated.
Estimates suggest that 7--17\% of recent scientific papers and peer reviews contain substantial LLM-modified content \cite{mapping_llm_science,monitoring_ai_review}, and this proportion continues to grow as generated text enters the web and becomes seed material for subsequent generation.
The result is recursive generation chains whose outputs progressively diverge from human-written text---a problem that current detection methods are ill-equipped to address.

Existing detectors \cite{fast_detectgpt,binoculars,ld_score,detectgpt} provide binary real-vs-synthetic classification, forcing an all-or-nothing filtering decision: discard everything flagged as synthetic, losing potentially useful first-generation content, or retain everything, admitting text with compounding distributional drift.
This conflates qualitatively different material.
A first-generation continuation---an LLM expanding a human-written passage---retains much of the source distribution's lexical and structural properties.
A third- or fourth-generation text, conditioned recursively on prior LLM outputs, exhibits measurably reduced vocabulary diversity, compressed perplexity, and narrower token probability distributions.
Treating these as a single ``synthetic'' category discards provenance information that could inform risk-stratified curation decisions.

We argue that a finer-grained characterization is needed: \emph{ordinal depth estimation}, the task of classifying text into generation depth classes (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+) rather than producing a binary label.
No existing method addresses this task directly.
When repurposed as ordinal depth predictors, individual detection scores exhibit high cross-generator variance---confidence intervals spanning 0.59--0.82 in macro-F1 (\S\ref{sec:results-baselines})---making any single detector unreliable across unknown generators.
Concurrent work on iterative paraphrasing chains \cite{broken_telephone,markovian_chains} analyzes convergence behavior under semantic-preservation constraints, which bound distinguishable depth classes to approximately three.
These results do not extend to \emph{non-paraphrastic} generation chains (e.g., continuation), where the absence of semantic anchoring permits richer depth signal.

We study distributional drift in non-paraphrastic LLM generation chains across six generators from three model families (Pythia, OLMo, Qwen; 0.6B--8B parameters).
Our central empirical finding is \emph{differential depth response}: central-tendency and diversity features---including reference-model mean entropy (functionally an NLL-based out-of-distribution score \cite{ood_baseline}), type-token ratio, and hapax ratio---drift monotonically with generation depth, while distributional shape features (entropy standard deviation, tail decay) remain near-stationary.
This pattern is consistent with recursive generation inducing a location shift in the NLL distribution: text becomes progressively more predictable on average while the functional form of the distribution is preserved.
The combination of drifting and stationary features yields a 7-feature ensemble that achieves leave-one-generator-out (LOGO) macro-F1 of 0.79 (95\% CI [0.786, 0.799]; \textit{plan-014}), with per-generator held-out F1 ranging from 0.69 to 0.85.

The practical advantage is reliability across unknown generators, not just average performance.

We also report a negative finding.
Depth-aware data curation---selecting training data based on estimated generation depth---does not improve downstream language model quality compared to random subsampling at equal sample count (perplexity: 2.367 random vs.\ 2.387 depth-stratified; \textit{plan-004-v2}).

\begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
    \item \textbf{Task formulation.} We define ordinal generation depth estimation as a task beyond binary detection, providing a framework for finer-grained provenance characterization of web-crawled text.

\section{Results}
\label{sec:results}

We evaluate depth fingerprinting along four axes: cross-generator classification (\S\ref{sec:results-classification}), differential depth response of individual features (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}), comparison with existing detection baselines (\S\ref{sec:results-baselines}), and downstream utility for data curation (\S\ref{sec:results-downstream}).

\subsection{Depth Classification Performance}
\label{sec:results-classification}

Table~\ref{tab:logo-results} reports leave-one-generator-out (LOGO) macro-F1 for 3-class depth estimation (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+) across six generators spanning three model families and parameter counts from 0.6B to 8.2B.

The 7-feature ensemble achieves LOGO F1\,=\,0.790 (95\% bootstrap CI [0.786, 0.799]), significantly outperforming all single-detector baselines ($p<0.001$; \S\ref{sec:results-baselines}).
Per-generator held-out F1 ranges from 0.685 (Qwen3-8B) to 0.855 (Pythia-1B).
Gen-0 classification is near-perfect (per-class F1\,$\approx$\,0.95); the primary difficulty lies in distinguishing gen-1 from gen-2+, where feature margins narrow.

\paragraph{Cross-scale transfer.}
The six-generator evaluation includes Qwen3-8B (8.2B parameters), confirming that depth signal persists at scales beyond the $\leq$2.8B training generators.
However, cross-scale transfer incurs a moderate gap: Qwen3-8B held-out F1\,=\,0.685 (CI [0.672, 0.698]), compared to 0.76--0.86 for $\leq$2.8B generators.
Text generated by larger models is more fluent, compressing feature margins and making depth distinctions harder.
Notably, adding Qwen3-8B data \emph{improves} classification on the original five generators (+0.9\,pp to 0.809), indicating that cross-scale diversity benefits rather than dilutes the training signal.

\paragraph{Cross-family generalization.}
Family-level leave-out (all Pythia generators held out, trained on OLMo + Qwen only) yields $\Delta$\,=\,+0.011 F1 relative to same-family LOGO, confirming that depth features transfer across architectural families without degradation.

\paragraph{Length confound control.}
Text length correlates weakly with depth (Spearman $|\rho| < 0.14$).
Length-normalized feature trends are preserved, and length-matched subsampling yields comparable or higher F1 ($\Delta$\,=\,+0.041), ruling out length as a confound (Appendix~\ref{app:length}).


\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{llcc}
\toprule
\textbf{Generator} & \textbf{Family} & \textbf{Params} & \textbf{Held-out F1} \\
\midrule
Pythia-1B       & Pythia & 1.0B & 0.855 \\
Pythia-2.8B     & Pythia & 2.8B & 0.804 \\
OLMo-2-1B      & OLMo   & 1.2B & 0.762 \\
Qwen3-0.6B     & Qwen   & 0.6B & 0.823 \\
Qwen3-1.7B     & Qwen   & 1.7B & 0.809 \\
Qwen3-8B       & Qwen   & 8.2B & 0.685 \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{3}{l}{Average (6-gen LOGO)} & 0.790 \\
\multicolumn{3}{l}{Average (5-gen, $\leq$2.8B)} & 0.804 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Leave-one-generator-out macro-F1 for 3-class depth estimation using the 7-feature ensemble. Each row holds out one generator for testing and trains on the remaining five. The 6-gen LOGO average (0.790, 95\% CI [0.786, 0.799]) includes Qwen3-8B, whose cross-scale transfer gap lowers the mean.}
\label{tab:logo-results}
\end{table}


\subsection{Differential Depth Response}
\label{sec:results-differential}

Features exhibit \emph{differential depth response}: central-tendency and diversity measures drift monotonically with depth, while distributional shape measures remain near-stationary.
This pattern is consistent with recursive generation inducing a location shift in the token-level NLL distribution---the text becomes progressively more predictable (mean shifts), while the functional form of the distribution is preserved (shape is invariant).

Individual-level Spearman correlations with depth confirm the split (Figure~\ref{fig:feature-drift}):
drifting features show strong monotonic trends (hapax ratio $\rho = -0.558$, TTR $\rho = -0.543$, entropy mean $\rho = -0.476$),
while shape features show weak or negligible correlations (entropy std $|\rho| = 0.076$, tail decay $|\rho| = 0.087$).

\paragraph{Feature complementarity.}
Table~\ref{tab:ablation} reports ablation results.
The full 7-feature set (F1\,=\,0.790) significantly outperforms both surface-only features (TTR + hapax; F1\,=\,0.729) and reference-only features (entropy statistics + tail decay; F1\,=\,0.745; McNemar $p \approx 0$).
Permutation importance ranks hapax ratio highest (0.271), followed by TTR (0.165) and entropy mean (0.156).
Surface features capture vocabulary impoverishment; reference features capture distributional shift---neither subsumes the other.

\paragraph{Cross-family reference models.}
To confirm that differential depth response is not an artifact of the Pythia-410M reference model, we compute features using three cross-family references: Pythia-410M, OLMo-2-1B, and Qwen3-0.6B.
All three achieve LOGO F1 between 0.80 and 0.82, with consistent drift directions across features.
The pattern generalizes across reference model architectures.


\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
\textbf{Feature set} & \textbf{LOGO F1} & \textbf{Top feature (importance)} \\
\midrule
Full (7 features)     & 0.790 & hapax\_ratio (0.271) \\
Surface only (2)      & 0.729 & hapax\_ratio (0.320) \\
Reference only (5)    & 0.745 & entropy\_mean (0.218) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Feature ablation (6-gen LOGO). Full $>$ surface = reference confirms complementarity between surface diversity features and reference-model distributional features.}
\label{tab:ablation}
\end{table}


\subsection{Comparison with Detection Baselines}
\label{sec:results-baselines}

We repurpose four existing detection scores as ordinal depth predictors by training the same ordinal classifier on each score as a single feature, using identical LOGO evaluation (Figure~\ref{fig:baseline-ci}).

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
\textbf{Method} & \textbf{LOGO F1} & \textbf{95\% CI} \\
\midrule
7-feature ensemble & \textbf{0.798} & [0.786, 0.799] \\
Avg-LogProb        & 0.765 & [0.616, 0.820] \\
LD-Score            & 0.721 & [0.588, 0.770] \\
FastDetectGPT       & 0.627 & [0.511, 0.762] \\
Binoculars          & 0.579 & [0.405, 0.664] \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Ordinal depth classification: 7-feature ensemble vs.\ single detection baselines (5-gen LOGO). The ensemble outperforms the best single detector (Avg-LogProb) by +3.9\,pp (paired bootstrap $p < 0.001$, $\Delta$ CI [3.4, 4.4]).}
\label{tab:baselines}
\end{table}

The ensemble outperforms all baselines in mean F1: +3.9\,pp over Avg-LogProb ($p < 0.001$, $\Delta$ CI [3.4, 4.4]), +7.7\,pp over LD-Score, +17.1\,pp over FastDetectGPT, and +21.9\,pp over Binoculars (Table~\ref{tab:baselines}).

The critical distinction is \emph{reliability}.
The ensemble CI spans just 1.3\,pp [0.786, 0.799], while single-detector CIs span 18--26\,pp (e.g., Avg-LogProb [0.616, 0.820]).
A single detector's CI is wider than \emph{all pairwise detector differences}, meaning no single detector is reliably best across generators.
Each detector captures partial depth signal---Avg-LogProb tracks mean perplexity shift, LD-Score captures character-level distributional change---but each fails on specific generator families.
The 7-feature ensemble aggregates complementary signals, producing stable performance regardless of the held-out generator.


\subsection{Downstream Utility: A Negative Finding}
\label{sec:results-downstream}

Can depth-aware data curation improve downstream language model quality?
We fine-tune OLMo-2-0425-1B on five data variants (3 seeds each) and evaluate perplexity on a held-out test set (Table~\ref{tab:downstream}).

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{lrc}
\toprule
\textbf{Variant} & \textbf{$n$} & \textbf{Test PPL} \\
\midrule
All depths            & 12{,}299 & 2.335 $\pm$ 0.000 \\
Size-matched (random) & 3{,}951  & 2.367 $\pm$ 0.000 \\
Depth 0--1 only       & 3{,}951  & 2.387 $\pm$ 0.001 \\
Binary-filtered       & 3{,}951  & 2.389 $\pm$ 0.000 \\
Depth 0 only          & 797      & 2.681 $\pm$ 0.001 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Downstream fine-tuning perplexity (OLMo-2-0425-1B, mean $\pm$ std across 3 seeds). At equal sample count, random subsampling (2.367) outperforms depth-aware curation (depth 0--1: 2.387, binary-filtered: 2.389).}
\label{tab:downstream}
\end{table}

The results are unambiguous: data quantity dominates depth composition.
Training on all 12{,}299 samples yields the lowest perplexity (2.335).
At equal sample count ($n$\,=\,3{,}951), random subsampling (2.367) \emph{outperforms} both depth-stratified selection (depth 0--1: 2.387) and binary detection filtering (2.389).
Cross-seed variance is below 0.002 across all variants, confirming the robustness of this null result.

Restricting training to human-only text (depth 0, $n$\,=\,797) produces a sharp perplexity increase to 2.681, driven primarily by the 5$\times$ reduction in data volume rather than depth composition per se.

We report this negative finding transparently: depth fingerprinting is an effective \emph{diagnostic} tool for characterizing text provenance, not a \emph{curative} tool for data curation.
Knowing the generation depth of a document does not, by itself, make it more or less useful for training.

\label{sec:conclusion}

Future work should extend evaluation to frontier-scale generators (70B+), mixed-generator chains that better approximate real-world contamination, and diverse prompt types beyond continuation.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Web-crawled corpora are the dominant source of pretraining data for large language models (LLMs), yet an increasing fraction of this data is itself LLM-generated.
Estimates suggest that 7--17\% of recent scientific papers and peer reviews contain substantial LLM-modified content \cite{mapping_llm_science,monitoring_ai_review}, and this proportion continues to grow as generated text enters the web and becomes seed material for subsequent generation.
The result is recursive generation chains whose outputs progressively diverge from human-written text---a problem that current detection methods are ill-equipped to address.

Existing detectors \cite{fast_detectgpt,binoculars,ld_score,detectgpt} provide binary real-vs-synthetic classification, forcing an all-or-nothing filtering decision: discard everything flagged as synthetic, losing potentially useful first-generation content, or retain everything, admitting text with compounding distributional drift.
This conflates qualitatively different material.
A first-generation continuation---an LLM expanding a human-written passage---retains much of the source distribution's lexical and structural properties.
A third- or fourth-generation text, conditioned recursively on prior LLM outputs, exhibits measurably reduced vocabulary diversity, compressed perplexity, and narrower token probability distributions.
Treating these as a single ``synthetic'' category discards provenance information that could inform risk-stratified curation decisions.

We argue that a finer-grained characterization is needed: \emph{ordinal depth estimation}, the task of classifying text into generation depth classes (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+) rather than producing a binary label.
No existing method addresses this task directly.
When repurposed as ordinal depth predictors, individual detection scores exhibit high cross-generator variance---confidence intervals spanning 0.59--0.82 in macro-F1 (\S\ref{sec:results-baselines})---making any single detector unreliable across unknown generators.
Concurrent work on iterative paraphrasing chains \cite{broken_telephone,markovian_chains} analyzes convergence behavior under semantic-preservation constraints, which bound distinguishable depth classes to approximately three.
These results do not extend to \emph{non-paraphrastic} generation chains (e.g., continuation), where the absence of semantic anchoring permits richer depth signal.

We study distributional drift in non-paraphrastic LLM generation chains across six generators from three model families (Pythia, OLMo, Qwen; 0.6B--8B parameters).
Our central empirical finding is \emph{differential depth response}: central-tendency and diversity features---including reference-model mean entropy (functionally an NLL-based out-of-distribution score \cite{ood_baseline}), type-token ratio, and hapax ratio---drift monotonically with generation depth, while distributional shape features (entropy standard deviation, tail decay) remain near-stationary.
This pattern is consistent with recursive generation inducing a location shift in the NLL distribution: text becomes progressively more predictable on average while the functional form of the distribution is preserved.
The combination of drifting and stationary features yields a 7-feature ensemble that achieves leave-one-generator-out (LOGO) macro-F1 of 0.79 (95\% CI [0.786, 0.799]; \textit{plan-014}), with per-generator held-out F1 ranging from 0.69 to 0.85.
This ensemble maintains tight cross-generator consistency (CI width 1.3\,pp), whereas the best single detector spans over 20\,pp (\textit{plan-015}).
The practical advantage is reliability across unknown generators, not just average performance.

We also report a negative finding.
Depth-aware data curation---selecting training data based on estimated generation depth---does not improve downstream language model quality compared to random subsampling at equal sample count (perplexity: 2.367 random vs.\ 2.387 depth-stratified; \textit{plan-004-v2}).
Depth fingerprinting is an effective \emph{diagnostic} tool for characterizing text provenance, not a \emph{curative} tool for data selection.

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
    \item \textbf{Task formulation.} We define ordinal generation depth estimation as a task beyond binary detection, providing a framework for finer-grained provenance characterization of web-crawled text.
    \item \textbf{Empirical characterization.} We document differential depth response across six generators spanning three model families (0.6B--8B): a 7-feature ensemble combining drifting and stationary features achieves LOGO F1\,=\,0.79 [0.786, 0.799], significantly outperforming all single-detector baselines ($p < 0.001$) with tight cross-generator consistency (\textit{plan-014, plan-015}).
    \item \textbf{Negative finding.} Depth-aware data curation does not outperform random subsampling for downstream CLM quality (size-matched 2.367 vs.\ depth-stratified 2.387; \textit{plan-004-v2}), establishing depth fingerprinting as diagnostic rather than curative.
\end{enumerate}

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Web-crawled corpora are the dominant source of pretraining data for large language models (LLMs), yet an increasing fraction of this data is itself LLM-generated.
Estimates suggest that 7--17\% of recent scientific papers and peer reviews contain substantial LLM-modified content \cite{mapping_llm_science,monitoring_ai_review}, and this proportion continues to grow as generated text enters the web and becomes seed material for subsequent generation.
The result is recursive generation chains whose outputs progressively diverge from human-written text---a problem that current detection methods are ill-equipped to address.

Existing detectors \cite{fast_detectgpt,binoculars,ld_score,detectgpt} provide binary real-vs-synthetic classification, forcing an all-or-nothing filtering decision: discard everything flagged as synthetic, losing potentially useful first-generation content, or retain everything, admitting text with compounding distributional drift.
This conflates qualitatively different material.
A first-generation continuation---an LLM expanding a human-written passage---retains much of the source distribution's lexical and structural properties.
A third- or fourth-generation text, conditioned recursively on prior LLM outputs, exhibits measurably reduced vocabulary diversity, compressed perplexity, and narrower token probability distributions.
Treating these as a single ``synthetic'' category discards provenance information that could inform risk-stratified curation decisions.

We argue that a finer-grained characterization is needed: \emph{ordinal depth estimation}, the task of classifying text into generation depth classes (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+) rather than producing a binary label.
No existing method addresses this task directly.
When repurposed as ordinal depth predictors, individual detection scores exhibit high cross-generator variance---confidence intervals spanning 0.41--0.82 in macro-F1 (\S\ref{sec:results-baselines})---making any single detector unreliable across unknown generators.
Concurrent work on iterative paraphrasing chains \cite{broken_telephone,markovian_chains} analyzes convergence behavior under semantic-preservation constraints, which bound distinguishable depth classes to approximately three.
These results do not extend to \emph{non-paraphrastic} generation chains (e.g., continuation), where the absence of semantic anchoring permits richer depth signal.

We study distributional drift in non-paraphrastic LLM generation chains across six generators from three model families (Pythia, OLMo, Qwen; 0.6B--8B parameters).
Our central empirical finding is \emph{differential depth response}: central-tendency and diversity features---including reference-model mean entropy (functionally an NLL-based out-of-distribution score \cite{ood_baseline}), type-token ratio, and hapax ratio---drift monotonically with generation depth, while distributional shape features (entropy standard deviation, tail decay) remain near-stationary.
This pattern is consistent with recursive generation inducing a location shift in the NLL distribution: text becomes progressively more predictable on average while the functional form of the distribution is preserved.
The combination of drifting and stationary features yields a 7-feature ensemble that achieves leave-one-generator-out (LOGO) macro-F1 of 0.79 (95\% CI [0.786, 0.799]; \textit{plan-014}), with per-generator held-out F1 ranging from 0.69 to 0.85.
This ensemble maintains tight cross-generator consistency (CI width 1.3\,pp), whereas the best single detector spans over 20\,pp (\textit{plan-015}).
The practical advantage is reliability across unknown generators, not just average performance.

We also report a negative finding.
Depth-aware data curation---selecting training data based on estimated generation depth---does not improve downstream language model quality compared to random subsampling at equal sample count (perplexity: 2.367 random vs.\ 2.387 depth-stratified; \textit{plan-004-v2}).
Depth fingerprinting is an effective \emph{diagnostic} tool for characterizing text provenance, not a \emph{curative} tool for data selection.

\begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
    \item \textbf{Task formulation.} We define ordinal generation depth estimation as a task beyond binary detection, providing a framework for finer-grained provenance characterization of web-crawled text.

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related}

\subsection{AI-Generated Text Detection}
\label{sec:related-detection}

Methods for distinguishing human-written from machine-generated text have evolved from statistical tests on token-level distributions \cite{gltr,grover,release_strategies} to zero-shot approaches exploiting reference-model likelihoods \cite{detectgpt,fast_detectgpt,binoculars,dna_gpt} and learned classifiers over linguistic features \cite{feat_aug_transformer,reliable_detection,ld_score}.
Recent work has pursued diverse detection signals: \citet{intrinsic_dimension} use intrinsic dimensionality estimates, \citet{diveye} propose surprisal diversity features directly comparable to our shape-based measures, and \citet{generator_barrier} characterize the distributional gap between human and model outputs.
\citet{jawahar_survey} provide a comprehensive survey.
A persistent limitation is that all these methods produce binary (real vs.\ synthetic) decisions.
Even when detection scores correlate with generation depth, they exhibit high cross-generator variance when repurposed as ordinal predictors (CI spanning 0.59--0.82 in macro-F1; \S\ref{sec:results-baselines}), because each score captures a single distributional property that generalizes inconsistently.
\citet{paraphrase_evades} and \citet{detection_possibilities} further demonstrate that detection robustness degrades under distributional shift.
Our reference-model entropy features are functionally NLL-based out-of-distribution scores \cite{ood_baseline}; the contribution is not a new detection method but the task formulation (ordinal depth estimation) and the empirical finding that combining drifting and stationary features yields consistent cross-generator performance.

\subsection{Model Collapse and Iterative Generation}
\label{sec:related-collapse}

A growing body of work studies quality degradation when models are trained on their own outputs.
\citet{self_consuming_mad} demonstrate that self-consuming generative models progressively lose distributional coverage, and \citet{curse_of_recursion} show that model collapse is inevitable in successive fine-tuning rounds without fresh human data, though \citet{model_collapse_avoidable} identify conditions under which careful data mixing can mitigate this effect.
\citet{strong_model_collapse} extend these results to larger-scale settings.
These studies focus on \emph{training-loop} degradation, where model weights are updated on recursive data.
Our setting is different: we study \emph{inference chains}, where a fixed model generates text conditioned on its own prior output without retraining.

Two concurrent lines of work are most directly relevant.
\citet{broken_telephone} analyze paraphrasing and translation chains, showing progressive information loss analogous to the telephone game.
\citet{markovian_chains} provide a theoretical framework for convergence in iterative text transformations, demonstrating that semantic-preservation constraints induce attractor dynamics that bound distinguishable depth to approximately three classes.
Our work differs in two respects: we study \emph{non-paraphrastic continuation} chains, where the absence of semantic anchoring permits richer depth signal beyond the attractor bound; and we focus on \emph{estimating} depth from text features rather than characterizing convergence behavior.

\subsection{Vocabulary Diversity and Stylometry}
\label{sec:related-diversity}

Declining lexical diversity in LLM-generated text is documented in both training \cite{curious_decline} and deployment \cite{writing_diversity} settings.
Our surface features---type-token ratio and hapax ratio---instantiate this observation for inference chains, where we show monotonic diversity decline across generation depths without any model retraining.

These features are classical stylometric measures with a long history in authorship attribution \cite{stamatatos_survey,koppel_authorship}.
\citet{uchendu_attribution} extend stylometric and neural methods to multi-class attribution of text to specific generators.
We push beyond generator identity to the \emph{depth} dimension: text from the same generator at different depths exhibits systematically different feature profiles, and these profiles generalize across generators.
Sampling strategies also affect diversity; \citet{nucleus_sampling} show that top-$p$ sampling mitigates some degeneration, but our results demonstrate that diversity still declines monotonically across recursive application of the same sampling procedure.

\subsection{Data Quality and Provenance}
\label{sec:related-provenance}

Scalable data curation relies on quality signals to filter web-crawled corpora.
\citet{dsir} select pretraining data to match a target distribution, \citet{qurating} learn quality scores from LLM judgments, and \citet{ccnet} filter Common Crawl via perplexity-based heuristics.
Generation depth is a complementary provenance signal: it characterizes \emph{how many steps removed} text is from a human source, orthogonal to content quality per se.

An alternative approach is proactive provenance through watermarking \cite{watermark_llm,synthid_text,aaronson_watermark}, where identifiable patterns are embedded during generation.
However, \citet{chainwash} demonstrate that watermark strength decays across multi-step generation chains, motivating passive post-hoc methods that do not require generator cooperation.
Our depth fingerprinting is such a method: it operates on text alone without assuming access to the generating model or an embedded watermark.
At the feature level, our reference-model NLL analysis connects to \citet{min_k_percent}, who use the probability distribution's lower tail for membership inference; we analyze the full NLL distribution for a different purpose---ordinal depth estimation rather than training-set membership.

\begin{abstract}
As large language model (LLM) outputs accumulate on the web, training corpora increasingly contain recursively generated text of unknown provenance depth.
We formulate \emph{ordinal depth estimation}---classifying whether text is human-written (gen-0), first-generation synthetic (gen-1), or deeper (gen-2+)---a task that moves beyond binary real-versus-synthetic detection.

\end{abstract}

\section*{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

Our experiments use generators up to 8.2B parameters (Qwen3-8B).
Depth signal persists at this scale, but cross-scale classifier transfer incurs a moderate gap (held-out F1\,=\,0.685 vs.\ 0.76--0.86 for $\leq$2.8B generators; \textit{plan-014}).
Frontier models (70B+) remain untested; their higher fluency may further compress feature margins.

All generation chains use a single prompt type (continuation).
Alternative chain types---elaboration, rewriting, summarization---may induce different drift patterns.
Prompt diversity experiments are planned but not yet completed.

Chains are constructed with a single generator model per chain.
Real-world web contamination likely involves heterogeneous generators at each step, which could attenuate or alter the depth signal we observe.

The negative downstream result (\S\ref{sec:results-downstream}) is evaluated on causal language modeling only.
Whether depth-aware curation affects other tasks (classification, summarization, instruction following) is not assessed.

We use 3-class granularity (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+).
Non-paraphrastic chains may support finer-grained depth distinctions, but we have not systematically evaluated classifiers at higher ordinal resolution.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Web-crawled corpora are the dominant source of pretraining data for large language models (LLMs), yet an increasing fraction of this data is itself LLM-generated.
Estimates suggest that 7--17\% of recent scientific papers and peer reviews contain substantial LLM-modified content \cite{mapping_llm_science,monitoring_ai_review}, and this proportion continues to grow as generated text enters the web and becomes seed material for subsequent generation.
The result is recursive generation chains whose outputs progressively diverge from human-written text---a problem that current detection methods are ill-equipped to address.

Existing detectors \cite{fast_detectgpt,binoculars,ld_score,detectgpt} provide binary real-vs-synthetic classification, forcing an all-or-nothing filtering decision: discard everything flagged as synthetic, losing potentially useful first-generation content, or retain everything, admitting text with compounding distributional drift.
This conflates qualitatively different material.
A first-generation continuation---an LLM expanding a human-written passage---retains much of the source distribution's lexical and structural properties.
A third- or fourth-generation text, conditioned recursively on prior LLM outputs, exhibits measurably reduced vocabulary diversity, compressed perplexity, and narrower token probability distributions.
Treating these as a single ``synthetic'' category discards provenance information that could inform risk-stratified curation decisions.

We argue that a finer-grained characterization is needed: \emph{ordinal depth estimation}, the task of classifying text into generation depth classes (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+) rather than producing a binary label.
No existing method addresses this task directly.
When repurposed as ordinal depth predictors, individual detection scores exhibit high cross-generator variance---confidence intervals spanning 0.59--0.82 in macro-F1 (\S\ref{sec:results-baselines})---making any single detector unreliable across unknown generators.
Concurrent work on iterative paraphrasing chains \cite{broken_telephone,markovian_chains} analyzes convergence behavior under semantic-preservation constraints, which bound distinguishable depth classes to approximately three.
These results do not extend to \emph{non-paraphrastic} generation chains (e.g., continuation), where the absence of semantic anchoring permits richer depth signal.

We study distributional drift in non-paraphrastic LLM generation chains across six generators from three model families (Pythia, OLMo, Qwen; 0.6B--8B parameters).
Our central empirical finding is \emph{differential depth response}: central-tendency and diversity features---including reference-model mean entropy (functionally an NLL-based out-of-distribution score \cite{ood_baseline}), type-token ratio, and hapax ratio---drift monotonically with generation depth, while distributional shape features (entropy standard deviation, tail decay) remain near-stationary.
This pattern is consistent with recursive generation inducing a location shift in the NLL distribution: text becomes progressively more predictable on average while the functional form of the distribution is preserved.
The combination of drifting and stationary features yields a 7-feature ensemble that achieves leave-one-generator-out (LOGO) macro-F1 of 0.79 (95\% CI [0.786, 0.799]; \textit{plan-014}), with per-generator held-out F1 ranging from 0.69 to 0.85.
This ensemble maintains tight cross-generator consistency (CI width 1.3\,pp), whereas the best single detector spans over 20\,pp (\textit{plan-015}).
The practical advantage is reliability across unknown generators, not just average performance.

We also report a negative finding.
Depth-aware data curation---selecting training data based on estimated generation depth---does not improve downstream language model quality compared to random subsampling at equal sample count (perplexity: 2.367 random vs.\ 2.387 depth-stratified; \textit{plan-004-v2}).
Depth fingerprinting is an effective \emph{diagnostic} tool for characterizing text provenance, not a \emph{curative} tool for data selection.

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
    \item \textbf{Task formulation.} We define ordinal generation depth estimation as a task beyond binary detection, providing a framework for finer-grained provenance characterization of web-crawled text.
    \item \textbf{Empirical characterization.} We document differential depth response across six generators spanning three model families (0.6B--8B): a 7-feature ensemble combining drifting and stationary features achieves LOGO F1\,=\,0.79 [0.786, 0.799], significantly outperforming all single-detector baselines ($p < 0.001$) with tight cross-generator consistency (\textit{plan-014, plan-015}).
    \item \textbf{Negative finding.} Depth-aware data curation does not outperform random subsampling for downstream CLM quality (size-matched 2.367 vs.\ depth-stratified 2.387; \textit{plan-004-v2}), establishing depth fingerprinting as diagnostic rather than curative.
\end{enumerate}

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows.
\S\ref{sec:related} surveys related work on text detection, model collapse, and data quality.
\S\ref{sec:method} describes generation chain construction, feature extraction, and evaluation protocol.
\S\ref{sec:results} presents classification results, differential depth response analysis, baseline comparisons, and the downstream utility experiment.
\S\ref{sec:discussion} discusses limitations and future directions.

\section{Related Work}

\subsection{AI-Generated Text Detection}

A large body of work addresses binary classification of machine-generated text.
Statistical approaches exploit token-level probability signals:
\cite{gltr} use token rank histograms under a reference model,
\cite{detectgpt} identify machine text through negative log-probability curvature,
and \cite{fast_detectgpt} accelerate this via conditional probability curvature.
\cite{binoculars} contrast perplexity ratios between two similar models,
while \cite{dna_gpt} measure n-gram divergence after re-generation.
More recent work extends these ideas:
\cite{ld_score} introduce character-distribution signatures orthogonal to perplexity,
\cite{intrinsic_dimension} leverage embedding-space intrinsic dimensionality,
and \cite{diveye} capture token surprisal diversity patterns.
Learned approaches include generator-specific discriminators \cite{grover},
feature-augmented transformers for cross-domain transfer \cite{feat_aug_transformer},
and disentangled representations for cross-generator generalization \cite{generator_barrier}.
Robustness analyses show that paraphrase attacks severely degrade detectors \cite{reliable_detection,paraphrase_evades},
though detection remains information-theoretically feasible whenever human and machine distributions are distinguishable \cite{detection_possibilities}.
\cite{jawahar_survey} and \cite{release_strategies} provide broader surveys.

These methods share a fundamental limitation: they produce a single binary score with no capacity for depth estimation.
When repurposed as ordinal depth predictors, individual detector scores exhibit high cross-generator variance (confidence intervals spanning 0.59--0.82 in our experiments), making them unreliable as standalone depth estimators.
Our reference-model entropy features are functionally NLL-based out-of-distribution scores \cite{ood_baseline}, drawing on the same signal backbone as DetectGPT and Binoculars.
The contribution is not the features themselves but rather the ordinal depth formulation, the empirical finding of differential depth response under recursive generation, and multi-feature complementarity that yields tight cross-generator consistency.

\subsection{Model Collapse and Iterative Generation}

Model collapse theory establishes that recursive training on synthetic data degrades generative quality.
\cite{curse_of_recursion} prove that iterative retraining causes irreversible distribution tail loss across VAEs, GMMs, and LLMs.
\cite{strong_model_collapse} show that even minimal synthetic data fractions suffice to trigger collapse,
\cite{self_consuming_mad} characterize precision--diversity trade-offs in autophagous loops,
and \cite{model_collapse_avoidable} demonstrate that data accumulation (rather than replacement) mitigates the effect.
These results concern \emph{training-loop} dynamics where model parameters change across iterations.
We study \emph{inference chains}: the same frozen model generates text recursively without retraining, yet distributional drift still accumulates.

Two concurrent works study iterative generation directly.
\cite{broken_telephone} analyze LLM paraphrasing and translation chains, showing that information distortion accumulates with depth and outputs converge toward attractor states---critically, the semantic-preservation constraint of paraphrasing bounds depth-distinguishable classes to approximately three.
\cite{markovian_chains} formalize this convergence, proving that iterative rephrasing chains either collapse to small cycle sets or continue producing novel sentences depending on temperature and initialization.
Both focus on \emph{paraphrastic} chains.
We study \emph{non-paraphrastic} continuation chains, where the absence of semantic anchoring permits richer depth signal, and formulate depth estimation as an explicit ordinal classification task rather than analyzing convergence behavior.

\subsection{Vocabulary Diversity and Stylometry}

Several studies document diversity decline in LLM-mediated text.
\cite{curious_decline} quantify lexical, syntactic, and semantic diversity loss across recursive fine-tuning iterations, finding particularly severe decline for creative tasks---the closest antecedent to our work, though they study training-loop effects rather than inference-chain drift and do not formulate depth estimation.
\cite{writing_diversity} show that LLM-assisted writing reduces inter-author diversity,
while \cite{mapping_llm_science} and \cite{monitoring_ai_review} estimate that 7--17\% of scientific papers and peer reviews contain substantial LLM-modified content.
\cite{nucleus_sampling} characterize neural text degeneration, proposing nucleus sampling whose truncation behavior shapes the distributional properties our features capture.

These works document diversity decline as a phenomenon but do not exploit it for depth classification.
Our surface features (type-token ratio, hapax ratio) are essentially stylometric, drawing on a long tradition of computational stylometry \cite{stamatatos_survey,koppel_authorship}.
\cite{uchendu_attribution} extend authorship attribution to neural text generator identification;
we further extend from \emph{source} attribution to \emph{depth} estimation, combining surface stylometric features with reference-model distributional features for complementary signal.

\subsection{Data Quality and Provenance}

Data curation pipelines increasingly rely on quality scoring to filter web-scale corpora.
\cite{ccnet} use language model perplexity for quality filtering,
\cite{dsir} apply importance resampling in n-gram feature space,
and \cite{qurating} employ LLM pairwise judgments for multi-dimensional quality assessment.
These methods score text quality but do not assess generation provenance or depth.

Watermarking offers an active provenance mechanism:
\cite{watermark_llm} embed statistical signals via green-list token biasing,
\cite{synthid_text} deploy production-scale watermarking,
and \cite{aaronson_watermark} propose pseudorandom function-based marking.
However, \cite{chainwash} demonstrate that multi-step rewriting chains reduce watermark detectability from 87.9\% to 4.86\% within five hops, motivating watermark-free approaches.
Depth fingerprinting complements both paradigms as a \emph{passive} provenance signal requiring no watermark embedding.
Methodologically, our probability-based features also connect to membership inference \cite{min_k_percent}, which analyzes token probability distributions for training set membership rather than generation depth.

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Why are shape features stationary?}
We observe that distributional shape features (entropy standard deviation, tail decay) remain near-stationary across generation depths, while central-tendency features drift monotonically (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}).
One \emph{speculative} explanation is that shape is primarily determined by the sampling mechanism (temperature, top-$p$ truncation) and the model's architecture-level output distribution, both of which are fixed across generation steps.
Recursive generation shifts \emph{what} the model talks about---steering toward higher-probability regions of the vocabulary---but does not alter \emph{how} the model distributes probability mass around its predictions.
If this account is correct, shape features should remain stationary even at much greater depths, while level features should continue to drift until reaching a fixed point.
We flag this as a hypothesis for future investigation, not a conclusion supported by our current experiments.

\paragraph{Practical implications.}
The differential depth response enables risk-stratified data curation.
Rather than the binary keep-or-discard decision imposed by existing detectors, practitioners can flag gen-2+ text for manual review while retaining gen-1 content that preserves much of the source distribution's properties.
The tight cross-generator consistency of the 7-feature ensemble (CI width 1.3\,pp; \textit{plan-015}) makes this feasible even when the generating model is unknown---the typical scenario for web-crawled data.

\paragraph{Information value of the negative finding.}
The downstream experiment (\S\ref{sec:results-downstream}) demonstrates that depth-aware curation does not improve language model quality over random subsampling at equal sample count (\textit{plan-004-v2}).
This negative result carries positive information value: it rules out depth-based filtering as a data selection strategy, sparing practitioners from investing in depth-conditional pipelines that would not yield quality gains.
The dominant factor is data quantity, not depth composition---a result consistent with scaling-law findings that emphasize the primacy of data volume \cite{self_consuming_mad}.

\paragraph{Connection to model collapse.}
Our results relate to, but are distinct from, model collapse \cite{curse_of_recursion,strong_model_collapse,self_consuming_mad}.
Model collapse describes distributional degradation when models are \emph{retrained} on their own outputs across generations.
We observe analogous distributional drift---monotonic decrease in vocabulary diversity, compression of perplexity---in \emph{inference chains} without any parameter updates.
This suggests that the drift mechanisms documented in model collapse theory (regression toward high-probability modes, loss of distributional tails) operate at inference time as well, driven by the sampling process rather than gradient updates.
The shared phenomenology motivates using depth fingerprinting features as early indicators of data that, if used for retraining, may accelerate model collapse.

Our central empirical finding is \emph{differential depth response}: central-tendency and diversity features---including reference-model mean entropy (functionally an NLL-based out-of-distribution score \cite{ood_baseline}), type-token ratio, and hapax ratio---drift monotonically with generation depth, while distributional shape features (entropy standard deviation, tail decay) remain near-stationary.
This pattern is consistent with recursive generation inducing a location shift in the NLL distribution: text becomes progressively more predictable on average while the functional form of the distribution is preserved.
The combination of drifting and stationary features yields a 7-feature ensemble that achieves leave-one-generator-out (LOGO) macro-F1 of 0.79, with per-generator held-out F1 ranging from 0.68 to 0.86.
This ensemble maintains tight cross-generator consistency (CI width 1.3\,pp), whereas the best single detector spans over 20\,pp.
The practical advantage is reliability across unknown generators, not just average performance.

We also report a negative finding.
Depth-aware data curation---selecting training data based on estimated generation depth---does not improve downstream language model quality compared to random subsampling at equal sample count (perplexity: 2.367 random vs.\ 2.387 depth-stratified).
Depth fingerprinting is an effective \emph{diagnostic} tool for characterizing text provenance, not a \emph{curative} tool for data selection.

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
    \item \textbf{Task formulation.} We define ordinal generation depth estimation as a task beyond binary detection, providing a framework for finer-grained provenance characterization of web-crawled text.
    \item \textbf{Empirical characterization.} We document differential depth response across six generators spanning three model families (0.6B--8B): a 7-feature ensemble combining drifting and stationary features achieves LOGO F1\,=\,0.79, significantly outperforming all single-detector baselines ($p < 0.001$) with tight cross-generator consistency.
    \item \textbf{Negative finding.} Depth-aware data curation does not outperform random subsampling for downstream CLM quality (size-matched 2.367 vs.\ depth-stratified 2.387; \textit{plan-004-v2}), establishing depth fingerprinting as diagnostic rather than curative.
\end{enumerate}

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows.
\S\ref{sec:related} surveys related work on text detection, model collapse, and data quality.
\S\ref{sec:method} describes generation chain construction, feature extraction, and evaluation protocol.
\S\ref{sec:results} presents classification results, differential depth response analysis, baseline comparisons, and the downstream utility experiment.
\S\ref{sec:discussion} discusses limitations and future directions.
